questions.title: Hours worked per worker per year in Germany
questions.hint: Richer societies have tended to take part of their gains as free time. Was that steady?
questions.explanation: It fell to 1,314 in 2020, from 2,181 in 1960.

questions.title: International trade as a share of GDP in the world
questions.unitLabel: exports plus imports of goods and services, % of GDP
questions.hint: Cheaper shipping and lower tariffs raise trade; recessions and swings in commodity prices move it too.
questions.explanation: It rose to 52% in 2020, from 26% in 1970. Exports and imports are added together, so each sale between countries counts twice, once on each side.

questions.title: Floor area of a typical new single-family house in the United States
questions.unitLabel: median square feet, new single-family houses completed
questions.hint: Think about what mortgage rates, land prices and smaller families each do to the houses builders choose to build.
questions.explanation: It went from 1,535 sq ft in 1975 to a high of 2,467 sq ft in 2015, then ended at 2,142 sq ft in 2025. From the Census Bureau and HUD Survey of Construction; it counts new houses only, including houses built for rent.

questions.title: Japanese yen you get for one US dollar
questions.hint: The end of fixed exchange rates in 1971, Japan’s export boom, the 1985 Plaza Accord, Japan’s bubble and lost decades, and a central bank that kept interest rates at zero while others raised theirs.
questions.explanation: It went from ¥227 in 1980 to a low of ¥88 in 2010, then ended at ¥132 in 2022. After the 1985 Plaza Accord, when the big economies agreed to push the dollar down, it fell from 238 yen to 128 by 1988, and a strong yen took it to a record low of 80 in 2011. Near-zero Japanese interest rates later sent it back up to 152 in 2024.

questions.title: Unemployment rate in the United Kingdom
questions.hint: Unemployment jumps in recessions and tends to come down more slowly than it went up.
questions.explanation: It fell to 4.0% in 2023, from 8.7% in 1995.
